title: Looping Through a Dictionary
objective: Visit every key, every value, or every pair in a dictionary using a for loop.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Calling .items() on a dictionary gives you each key and its value together, which you can unpack into two loop variables at once.
.keys() loops through just the keys, and .values() loops through just the values — looping over the dictionary itself gives you the keys by default.
Dictionaries don't guarantee any particular order. If you need the keys in a predictable order, wrap the loop in sorted(), e.g. for key in sorted(forge.keys()).
explanation.rule: Use .items() for pairs, .keys() for keys, .values() for values — and sorted() when order matters.

examples.title: Reading the Ledger
examples.note: items() unpacks into (key, value) pairs; sorted(prices.keys()) visits the keys alphabetically.

checks.question: Which loop header visits only the values stored in a dictionary called stock?

feedback.correct: Right — .values() gives you just the values, without their keys.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — that form gives you something other than just the values.

assignment.title: Total Order
assignment.brief: Write total_cost(prices) that takes a dictionary of item name to price, and prints the total of all the values using a for loop (not sum()).
requirements: Loop over the dictionary's values with a for loop.
Do not use the built-in sum() function.
